class.name: PhysXFlow3D
class.brief_description: NVIDIA Flow smoke, fire and dust, provided by the PhysX module.
class.description: Simulates gas with NVIDIA Flow: a sparse, unbounded grid (it grows wherever the gas goes) with pressure projection, vorticity confinement and combustion. It's fed by the [PhysXFlowEmitter3D] nodes whose [member PhysXFlowEmitter3D.flow] points at it (or, with none set, by every emitter when this is the scene's only [PhysXFlow3D]); physics bodies within [member collision_range] of those emitters are solids the gas flows around, and moving bodies push it. Flow runs on Godot's own [RenderingDevice] (Vulkan or Direct3D 12), and [PhysXFlowRenderEffect] draws it into the frame with Flow's own ray marcher, self-shadowed by the scene's first visible [DirectionalLight3D] -- straight from the GPU, at the simulation's full resolution. Nothing is read back to the CPU unless [member cpu_readback] is on. The render effect is installed by itself, without touching anything you save: with no [Compositor] in the world one is created on the [World3D] while flows exist, and a [Compositor] of your own (on a [WorldEnvironment] or [Camera3D]) gets the effect added at the rendering-server level only -- its effects array is never modified. All of it is undone when the world's last flow leaves. [b]Requirements:[/b] an engine built with [code]flow_sdk=[/code], [code]nvflow.dll[/code] and [code]nvflowext.dll[/code] next to the executable (they are loaded at run time -- without them this node shows a warning and stays inert), and the Forward+ or Mobile renderer (not Compatibility, not headless). Flow's shaders are compiled the first time each is used (a fraction of a second on a first run) and kept in Godot's shader cache folder. [b]Units:[/b] meters and m/s, like the rest of the scene; Flow's own tuned defaults are converted at the boundary.

method.name: get_stats
method.description: Diagnostics: [code]running[/code], [code]error[/code], [code]start_ms[/code] (grid creation), [code]step_ms[/code], [code]render_calls[/code], [code]render_outputs[/code], [code]readback_bytes[/code], [code]bounds[/code] (the gas, with [member cpu_readback]), [code]active_blocks[/code] (sparse blocks in use, of [member max_blocks]), and Flow's pipeline / pass / resource counts.

method.name: is_running
method.description: Whether Flow is running for this node (see the configuration warnings if not).

method.name: sample_smoke
method.description: The smoke at [param position] (world space), from the last CPU readback. Needs [member cpu_readback]; returns [code]-1.0[/code] without it. The readback lags a few frames behind the simulation.

members.member: Upward acceleration per unit of temperature: hot gas rises, cool gas hangs. "Up" is opposite the project's default gravity.
Simulation cell size in meters. Smaller is finer detail and more GPU cost.
Physics bodies near the gas become solids for it. Box, sphere, capsule and cylinder shapes are supported; convex, concave and heightmap shapes are not yet.
The physics layers whose bodies the gas collides with.
How far from this flow's emitters (in meters) bodies are looked for. With [member cpu_readback] on, the area the gas has spread to is searched as well.
Fuel burns when hotter than [member ignition_temperature], releasing heat and smoke.
How fast the gas cools (exponential, per second).

Copy temperature and smoke back to the CPU every few steps, for [method sample_smoke] and the [code]bounds[/code] in [method get_stats]. Off by default: it costs a full field copy each time and isn't needed for rendering.
How bright the [member heat_ramp] glow is. [code]0[/code] turns glowing off.

How the gas glows by temperature, from [code]0[/code] to [member temperature_range]: each color is the glow at that temperature, its alpha how much it glows instead of showing the lit smoke. Empty uses a built-in fire ramp (transparent when cool, deep orange when warm, yellow-white when hot).
The temperature above which fuel burns (see [member combustion]).

The most sparse blocks the gas may take up -- a GPU memory budget, since Flow reserves memory for all of them when the grid starts (about 0.45 MB a block: the default 1024 is roughly 0.5 GB). A small plume uses a few hundred; [method get_stats] reports [code]active_blocks[/code]. Gas that would need more is cut off, with a warning. Changing it restarts the simulation.

How far the self-shadowing reaches toward the light, in steps of three quarters of a cell (48 is about 1.8 m at the default [member cell_size]). Too few for the gas's width leaves it lit almost evenly. [code]0[/code] turns self-shadowing off.
The smoke's color, lit by the scene's sun: white steam, gray or black smoke, brown dust, colored signal smoke. See also [member smoke_ramp].
Opacity per meter, per unit of smoke. Burning fuel makes a lot of smoke, so fire reads dense at the default; plain smoke or dust emitters may want 2-10.
How fast smoke thins out (per second). Lower values let it climb and linger longer.

The smoke's color by temperature, from [code]0[/code] to [member temperature_range] -- e.g. black soot near a fire turning light gray as it cools. Empty uses [member smoke_color] at every temperature. Alpha is ignored (opacity comes from the smoke itself).
The temperature at the end of [member heat_ramp].
Vorticity confinement: keeps small swirls alive for rolling, billowing gas.
